title: Serbia's Restless Dead
description: Two Habsburg reports, from 1725 and 1732, that taught educated Europe the word vampire

concepts.title: Kisilova, 1725
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1725 an imperial official named Ernst Frombald, a Kameralprovisor of the Gradiška district, was called to the village of Kisilova, probably modern Kisiljevo in eastern Serbia. The region had passed from Ottoman to Habsburg rule at the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718, and it would return to the Ottomans in 1739. A peasant named Petar Blagojević, written Peter Plogojowitz in the German report, had died and been buried. Within eight days, nine villagers died after illnesses of about a day. Before dying, they said Blagojević had come to them at night and throttled them. His widow said he had visited her to ask for his opanci, peasant shoes, and she moved to another village.

The villagers demanded permission to open the grave at once. Otherwise, they said, they would abandon the village, as they claimed had happened in the time of Turkish rule. Frombald gave way and attended with the parish priest of Veliko Gradište. His report describes a body that did not look decayed: hair and beard grown, the old skin peeled away with fresh skin beneath, new nails, and fresh blood in the mouth. The villagers drove a sharpened stake into the chest, and blood ran from the ears and mouth. Then they burned the body.

Frombald presented his consent as reluctant, given under pressure from terrified people. His account was printed in the Vienna newspaper Wienerisches Diarium on 21 July 1725, and it gave German readers a local word for such a corpse, rendered as vampyri.

concepts.title: Arnold Paole and Medveđa
concepts.contentHtml:
A larger case followed in the winter of 1731 to 1732 at Medveđa, a village near the West Morava River home to Serbian frontier militiamen, the hajduks. As deaths mounted, the Habsburg command sent Glaser, a "contagion physician" who watched for epidemics. On 12 December 1731 he found no sign of a contagious disease and blamed hunger and harsh fasting. But villagers had accused two of the recent dead, women named Miliza and Stana, and were threatening to leave. Glaser opened graves, found most bodies undecayed, and advised giving the villagers their way.

A second commission under the military surgeon Johann Flückinger opened the graves on 7 January 1732 and heard an older story. About five years before, a hajduk named Arnold Paole had broken his neck falling from a hay wagon. He had once said that a vampire troubled him at a place called Gossowa, perhaps Kosovo, in Ottoman Serbia, and that he cured himself by eating earth from its grave. Within 20 or 30 days four people complained that he was tormenting them, and they died. Forty days after his death villagers opened his grave, judged him fresh, staked him and burned him with his four supposed victims. Paole, they added, had also preyed on cattle, so people who ate the meat became vampires too.

Flückinger's surgeons dissected the recent dead and judged most to be in the "vampire condition," with fresh blood and new nails. Romani laborers beheaded those bodies and burned them, and the ashes went into the river. The report, signed in Belgrade on 26 January 1732 by Flückinger and four colleagues, was headed Visum et Repertum, Latin for "seen and discovered," a standard heading for medical findings.

concepts.title: Europe Reads About Vampires
concepts.contentHtml:
Medveđa became the vampire case for educated Europe. In February 1732 Glaser's father sent a letter about it to a Nuremberg medical journal, the Commercium Litterarium, and the report itself was printed in Nuremberg that year. Gazettes across the continent summarized it, and the word vampire appears in French-language and English periodicals by March 1732. By one count, sixteen formal treatises and dissertations, most by German doctors and theologians, debated the case. The German clergyman Michael Ranft expanded his Latin study of the "chewing and smacking of the dead in their graves" into a German book in 1734.

The writers argued over causes as much as belief. Some saw the devil at work, some proposed a natural sympathy between a corpse and its living kin, and others blamed terror and the misreading of bodies. The Benedictine scholar Antoine Augustin Calmet, from Lorraine, gathered the reports in a treatise first published in 1746 and expanded in 1751; his verdict was cautious and hard to pin down, and Voltaire mocked him for taking the stories seriously. Pope Benedict XIV, in a 1749 edition of his work on canonization, put such cases down to nature, imagination and fear.

The Habsburgs ended the matter by law. In 1755 Empress Maria Theresa sent her physician Gerard van Swieten to look into vampire reports from Moravia. He blamed natural processes and called the belief a "barbarism of ignorance," and she then banned the old remedies of opening graves, staking, beheading and burning. The figure lived on in literature instead: John Polidori's The Vampyre (1819) and Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897) turned a swollen village corpse into an aristocrat.

title: Reading the Corpse
description: What decay does to a body, and what archaeologists find in so-called vampire graves

concepts.title: What the Diggers Saw
concepts.contentHtml:
The folklorist Paul Barber, in Vampires, Burial, and Death (1988), took the Serbian reports seriously as observations and asked what the diggers had actually seen. His answer, drawn from forensic pathology, is that nearly every sign of a "vampire" is a normal stage of decomposition that most people never watch up close.

After death, bacteria in the gut produce gas and the body swells, so a thin corpse can look plump and well fed, its face flushed and dark. Gas pressure pushes bloody fluid from the lungs up through the nose and mouth, which looks like fresh blood from a recent meal. Blood can become liquid again after death, so it may flow when a body is cut or pierced. The outer layer of skin slips away, exposing a pinkish layer beneath, which Frombald recorded as "new skin"; nails loosen and fall off, leaving nail beds that resemble new nails. As skin dries and shrinks back, hair, beard and nails seem to have grown. When a stake forces trapped gas out past the vocal cords, the body can make a sound, the "groan" reported at Medveđa.

Timing mattered too. Decay runs fast in warm air and slowly in cold, wet or airless soil, so a body opened weeks after burial in a Balkan winter might look fresher than expected while its neighbor had rotted. Barber's point was not that villagers were fools. Their reasoning was consistent: they knew roughly what a corpse should look like, and these did not match. The vampire of folklore was a swollen, ruddy peasant in a shroud, not a pale count in evening dress.

concepts.title: Sickles at Drawsko
concepts.contentHtml:
The same fears turn up in the ground. At Drawsko, a village in northwestern Poland, excavations from 2008 to 2012 uncovered a cemetery of the 17th and 18th centuries holding about 285 skeletons. Six burials stood out. Five had an iron sickle laid across the throat or abdomen, and two had large stones placed under the chin. One common reading, drawn from regional folklore, is that a corpse trying to sit up would cut itself on the blade, and that a stone would keep the jaw shut and the dead in place.

One hypothesis held that the six were outsiders, since newcomers were often suspected of being dangerous. In 2014 a team led by the bioarchaeologist Lesley Gregoricka tested that idea with strontium isotopes. Strontium from local rock and water is laid down in tooth enamel during childhood, so it records where a person grew up. All five deviant burials that could be tested had local values. The people treated with suspicion were neighbors, not migrants.

The team suggested that the first people to die in an infectious outbreak might be blamed for the deaths that followed, a pattern that matches the Serbian cases. The idea is hard to test, because many epidemic diseases leave no trace on bone. The six also lay inside the ordinary cemetery, among everyone else. Precaution, rather than punishment, may be the better word for what their families or neighbors did.

concepts.title: Padlocks, Bricks and Caution
concepts.contentHtml:
Other finds have drawn headlines. In the late summer of 2022, archaeologists at Pień, a village near Bydgoszcz in north-central Poland, uncovered the grave of a young woman in an early modern cemetery, usually dated to the 17th century. A sickle had been placed across her neck and a triangular padlock fastened to a toe of her left foot, perhaps to lock her in the grave. In 2024 a forensic reconstruction gave her a face. In 2012 Bulgarian archaeologists at Sozopol, on the Black Sea, reported medieval burials with iron driven through the chest. In 2009 an Italian anthropologist described a 16th-century woman from a plague burial ground on the island of Lazzaretto Nuovo, in the Venetian lagoon, with a brick in her mouth. He linked it to belief in "shroud-eaters," corpses thought to chew their burial cloth and spread plague.

Specialists urge caution. "Vampire burial" is a modern label, and the people who placed a sickle or a stone left no note explaining it. Archaeologists such as Leszek Gardeła have argued that many unusual graves in Poland held people feared for other reasons, such as suicides, executed criminals or victims of a sudden "bad death," and that rites to keep dangerous dead in place are older and broader than the vampire. Face-down burial, decapitation and stones on the body occur across Europe from prehistory onward.

The written and buried evidence also show different practices. The Serbian reports describe opening and destroying a suspect after deaths had begun. The Polish graves show precautions taken at burial, before anyone was accused. Both rest on the idea that some dead are dangerous, but they are not the same rite.

title: New England's Vampire Panic
description: Tuberculosis, burned hearts and a Rhode Island family in 1892

concepts.title: Mercy Brown, 1892
concepts.contentHtml:
The most famous American "vampire" case came ten years after the German physician Robert Koch announced, in 1882, the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. The Brown family of Exeter, Rhode Island, had been struck by consumption, the old name for the disease. Mary Eliza Brown, the mother, died in December 1883, and the eldest daughter, Mary Olive, in June 1884. In 1891 the son, Edwin, and another daughter, Mercy Lena Brown, fell ill. Mercy died in January 1892, aged 19 according to her gravestone, while Edwin grew steadily weaker.

Neighbors pressed the father, George Brown, to try an old remedy. On 17 March 1892 a group that included the local doctor, Harold Metcalf, and a newspaper reporter opened the family graves. The mother and elder daughter had decayed as expected. Mercy had been dead only about two months, through a New England winter. The doctor saw ordinary decomposition, but her heart, when cut open, still held blood, and to those who feared her that was the sign they sought. Her heart and liver were removed and burned, and the ashes were mixed into a drink for Edwin. The remedy failed, and he died within about two months.

Newspapers reported the exhumation with curiosity and scorn, as a relic of old superstition surviving in a modern state. Mercy was reburied in the cemetery of the Baptist church in Exeter, where her grave still draws visitors. Some writers suggest that Bram Stoker read about the case before he published Dracula in 1897, but the link is unproven.

concepts.title: Consumption and the Family Cure
concepts.contentHtml:
Tuberculosis was one of the great killers of 19th-century New England. It spreads through the air, most easily within a household, and can take years to kill. Before the germ was understood, the pattern looked like this: one family member dies of consumption, and then a brother, a sister or a parent begins to waste away in the same way, as if the dead were drawing the life out of the living.

The New England remedy followed from that logic. A family opened the grave of an earlier victim and looked for signs that the corpse was still active, such as liquid blood in the heart. They burned the heart or other organs, and sometimes the sick swallowed the ashes or breathed the smoke. Recorded cases run from the 1780s to the 1890s, mostly in Rhode Island, eastern Connecticut, southern Massachusetts and Vermont. In 1793, at Manchester, Vermont, the body of Rachel Harris Burton was exhumed in an attempt to save her widower's second wife. At South Woodstock, Vermont, the heart of Frederick Ransom, who died of tuberculosis on 14 February 1817 at the age of 20, was burned on a blacksmith's forge because his father feared for the rest of the family.

The folklorist Michael Bell, who spent decades tracking these cases, stresses that families rarely used the word "vampire," and that no credible account describes a corpse leaving its grave to drink blood. Newspapers supplied the European label. The practice was a desperate family medical measure, often urged by neighbors. In his journal for 26 September 1859, Henry David Thoreau noted one such case and wrote, "The savage in man is never quite eradicated."

concepts.title: The Grave Marked JB 55
concepts.contentHtml:
The physical evidence for the practice came to light by accident. In 1990 children playing in a gravel pit in Griswold, Connecticut, dislodged human skulls. Connecticut's state archaeologist, Nicholas Bellantoni, and his team excavated a forgotten family burial ground of the 18th and 19th centuries. Most burials were ordinary. One coffin had "JB 55" spelled out in tacks on its lid, a common way of marking a person's initials and age at death.

Inside, the bones had been rearranged long after the body decayed. The skull and thigh bones lay on the chest in a skull-and-crossbones pattern. Lesions on the ribs suggested a chronic lung infection, possibly tuberculosis. In a 1994 paper the excavators read the grave as a New England "vampire" case: someone had reopened it, probably after more deaths in the family, found no heart left to burn, and broke up the skeleton instead.

In 2019 Y-chromosome DNA pointed to the surname Barber, and newspaper records led researchers to a farmer named John Barber; further DNA work presented in 2022 supported the identification. A nearby coffin marked "NB 13" probably belonged to his son Nathan, who died in 1826 at about 13. The family that feared him still laid his bones back in the coffin, in the family plot, among his kin.

title: The Werewolf Trials
description: Courts in France, Germany and Livonia that tried people as wolves, and the doubters who disagreed

concepts.title: The Hermit of Dole, 1573
concepts.contentHtml:
In the early 1570s the Franche-Comté, then a Habsburg-ruled county in what is now eastern France, was alarmed by children found dead or missing in the countryside around Dole. In 1573 the parlement of Dole, the province's high court, authorized local people to gather and hunt down the "werewolf" responsible. Suspicion fell on Gilles Garnier, a poor recluse said to come from the Lyon area, who lived near Amange with his wife and children and struggled to feed them.

Garnier confessed, probably under torture, to killing four children aged about 9 to 12 over several months and to eating parts of some of them. He said a spirit had appeared to him in the woods and given him an ointment that let him take the shape of a wolf. More than 50 witnesses testified against him, some saying they had seen him as a man and some as a wolf. The court convicted him of "lycanthropy and witchcraft," and he was burned at Dole on 18 January 1574. A printed account of the judgment appeared the same year, which is how the case spread.

The case shows how a werewolf trial worked. Real deaths came first, and the court then sought a person to answer for them. The transformation story turned a charge of murder into a crime against God, joined to witchcraft through the ointment. Whether Garnier killed anyone cannot now be tested.

concepts.title: The Bedburg Werewolf, 1589
concepts.contentHtml:
The most notorious werewolf case is that of Peter Stumpp, also spelled Stubbe or Stübbe, a farmer of Bedburg near Cologne. On 31 October 1589 he was put to death with great cruelty after confessing, on the rack, to 25 years of killings whose victims included children and two pregnant women, along with incest and dealings with a demon. He said the devil had given him a belt that turned him into a wolf; it was never found. His daughter and his mistress were executed with him, and his head was set on a pole above the execution wheel with the carved figure of a wolf, as a warning.

Most of these details come from a 16-page English pamphlet printed in London in 1590, which claimed to translate a German report that does not survive. Only two copies are known, and the occultist Montague Summers made the case famous by reprinting the pamphlet in his book The Werewolf (1933). Other sources, including the diary of the Cologne alderman Hermann von Weinsberg and German illustrated broadsheets, confirm that a man was executed as a werewolf. The lurid particulars are harder to trust.

Historians read the case against its setting. The Cologne War of 1583 to 1588, fought over whether the archbishop of Cologne could turn Protestant and keep his lands, had just swept the Rhineland, and Stumpp was probably a Protestant. Some writers argue that he was an innocent victim of that conflict or of local enmity; others accept that he was a killer whose crimes were dressed in demonology. The surviving evidence cannot settle the question.

concepts.title: Hounds of God and Doubting Doctors
concepts.contentHtml:
Werewolf trials were a small corner of the witch hunts. The historian Elmar Lorey counted about 280 known cases between 1407 and 1725, with a peak between about 1575 and 1657, mostly in French and German-speaking lands, the Low Countries and the Baltic. They began with the early 15th-century witch trials of Valais and Vaud, in modern Switzerland. In the Jura, Henri Boguet, the chief judge of Saint-Claude from 1596 to 1616, tried several accused werewolves and wrote a handbook on witches (1602) that was reprinted many times. Later legend credited him with as many as 1,500 victims; the true figure was probably about forty.

Some accused told stories that fit no judge's scheme. In 1692 at Jürgensburg in Livonia, now in Latvia, a man in his eighties named Thiess told the court that he was indeed a werewolf, but one of the "hounds of God." On three nights a year, St Lucy's, Midsummer and Pentecost, werewolves went to hell with iron rods to fight the witches and win back the grain and livestock they had stolen. The judges had him flogged and banished. The historian Carlo Ginzburg compared him to the benandanti of Friuli, villagers who said they fought witches in spirit at night, and read both as survivals of older shamanic belief. Others, such as Willem de Blécourt, dispute that reading.

Physicians offered another explanation. Greek medical writers of the Roman era described lykanthropia as a form of melancholy whose sufferers believed they were wolves and haunted tombs at night. In the 16th century the physician Johann Weyer argued that many accused witches and werewolves were deluded or ill, not guilty. Psychiatrists still occasionally report the delusion, called clinical lycanthropy.

title: The Beast of Gévaudan
description: Three years of attacks in the French uplands, a bishop's letter, the king's hunters and a press sensation

concepts.title: A Killer in the Hills
concepts.contentHtml:
On 30 June 1764 Jeanne Boulet, aged 14, was killed by an animal near Langogne in the Gévaudan, a poor upland district of southern France roughly matching the modern department of Lozère. Over the next three years attacks spread across an area about 90 by 80 kilometers, falling mostly on children and young women who watched livestock in the fields. Witnesses described a beast larger than a wolf, the size of a calf, with reddish fur, a dark stripe along the back and a long tail ending in a tuft.

The toll is uncertain. One detailed count lists 210 attacks, 113 deaths and 49 injuries between 1764 and 1767; other estimates put the deaths at roughly 60 to 100. Some victims fought back. On 12 January 1765 a boy named Jacques Portefaix and a group of other children drove the animal off at Villaret, and King Louis XV rewarded them and paid for Portefaix's education. On 11 August 1765 Marie-Jeanne Vallet, a young woman of about 20, wounded it with a spear.

The bishop of Mende, Gabriel-Florent de Choiseul-Beaupré, gave the disaster a religious frame. In a pastoral letter dated 31 December 1764 he presented the attacks as a scourge for the people's sins and ordered public prayers and penance, including the Forty Hours devotion, on three Sundays. In the parishes, the beast could be an animal and a divine judgment at the same time. Prayer and the hunt went on together, and so did rumor: some called the creature a sorcerer who could turn aside bullets, though the word werewolf seems almost never to have been used of it at the time.

concepts.title: The King's Hunters
concepts.contentHtml:
The beast became a test of royal power. Captain Duhamel led dragoons against it in late 1764 and early 1765 without success. In February 1765 the professional wolf-hunter Jean-Charles d'Enneval and his son arrived with bloodhounds, and they too failed. In June the king sent his own gun-bearer, François Antoine. On 20 or 21 September 1765, near the abbey of Chazes, Antoine killed a very large gray wolf, about 60 kilograms by one report. It was sent to Versailles, the court declared the beast dead, and Antoine went home richly rewarded.

The killings did not stop. After a quiet November, attacks resumed in December 1765, but the court had lost interest and the newspapers largely dropped the story. Local nobles and peasants kept hunting. On 19 June 1767, during a hunt organized by the Marquis d'Apcher, a local man named Jean Chastel shot a large wolf-like animal on Mont Mouchet, and the attacks then ceased. A notary's report of its examination, found again in the archives in 1952, describes it in detail, down to its teeth.

The most famous detail is a later invention. Chastel is often said to have loaded his gun with blessed silver bullets, a story that turns the hunt into a contest between good and evil. It comes from the 20th-century writer Henri Pourrat, not from any 18th-century source.

concepts.title: Wolf, Hybrid or Media Monster?
concepts.contentHtml:
Theories about the beast have multiplied for 250 years: an escaped lion or hyena, a wolf-dog hybrid trained by a human master, a human killer disguised in skins. None has firm documentary support. The historian Jean-Marc Moriceau, who cataloged some 3,000 wolf attacks on people in France between the 15th and 20th centuries, argues that the Gévaudan deaths fit the known pattern of attacks by wolves, probably more than one animal, on young herders in open country. Such attacks were not rare: in the spring of 1765 a wolf near Soissons, in northern France, killed at least four people.

The historian Jay M. Smith, in Monsters of the Gévaudan (2011), argues that the beast as a single monster was partly made in print. Newspapers such as the Courrier d'Avignon turned scattered rural deaths into a running national story, readers in Paris and abroad followed each episode, and by April 1765 English journalists were mocking the French king's failure to kill one animal. This came only two years after France's defeat in the Seven Years' War (1756 to 1763), when royal prestige was already bruised. Each new sighting was described in terms set by earlier reports.

Religious and secular readings ran side by side. The bishop saw a scourge; officials saw a pest to destroy; the press saw a serial drama. Real deaths, a single named monster and amplification by print make the Gévaudan a forerunner of what sociologists later called a moral panic.

title: Changelings and the Logic of Panic
description: Fairy substitutes, the death of Bridget Cleary in 1895, and what 'moral panic' does and does not explain

concepts.title: The Child Who Was Not Yours
concepts.contentHtml:
Across Ireland, Scotland, Scandinavia and the German lands, folk belief held that fairies, trolls or the devil might steal a human baby and leave a substitute, a changeling. The swapped child was sickly, cried constantly and failed to grow or speak, yet ate greedily. The substitute might be an ancient fairy in disguise, or a piece of wood shaped like the child. Martin Luther, in table talk recorded around 1540, called such a child a soulless "lump of flesh" and said the devil laid such creatures in cradles in place of real children. The same fear lay behind the medieval rite at the shrine of the greyhound Saint Guinefort.

The belief came with remedies meant to force an exchange. A family might trick the changeling into revealing its age, for instance by brewing in eggshells until it exclaimed that in all its long life it had never seen such a thing. Or they threatened it with fire, water or a hot oven, so that its own people would take it back and return the human child. Iron and baptism were thought to protect an infant; in Scandinavia parents laid iron tools on the cradles of unbaptized babies.

Sometimes the threats were carried out. In 1826, in County Kerry, Ireland, a woman named Anne Roche bathed Michael Leahy, a four-year-old who could neither speak nor stand, three times in the River Flesk to drive the fairy out of him, and he drowned. A jury acquitted her of murder. Many scholars think changeling stories gave words to families whose children were disabled or ill, though the disability historians Goodey and Stainton warn against mapping modern diagnoses onto the folklore.

concepts.title: Bridget Cleary, 1895
concepts.contentHtml:
The best-documented changeling killing came in late Victorian Ireland. Bridget Cleary, born Bridget Boland and aged about 26, was a dressmaker at Ballyvadlea in County Tipperary who kept her own hens and sold eggs. She had married Michael Cleary, a cooper, in 1887, and the couple lived with her father in a house built on the site of a supposed fairy ringfort. In March 1895 she fell ill with what a doctor diagnosed as bronchitis, and a priest gave her the last rites.

Her husband and several relatives and neighbors came to say that the sick woman was not Bridget but a fairy substitute. Over several nights they forced remedies on her and threatened her to make the changeling leave. On 15 March 1895 Michael Cleary killed her; the coroner's inquest found that she died of burning. He claimed she had gone with the fairies, and witnesses said he waited at a nearby fairy fort to win her back. Her body was found in a shallow grave on 22 March.

In July 1895 Michael Cleary was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 20 years of penal servitude. He served 15 and emigrated to Montreal after his release in 1910; several relatives received shorter terms. The case broke during the fight over Irish Home Rule, and opponents of self-government cited it as proof of Irish backwardness. The folklorist Angela Bourke, in The Burning of Bridget Cleary (1999), reads fairy belief as a language for illness, marriage and a young woman's independence. Whether Michael believed his own story is debated. A rhyme remembered in Tipperary asks, "Are you a witch, or are you a fairy, or are you the wife of Michael Cleary?"

concepts.title: What a Moral Panic Explains
concepts.contentHtml:
The sociologist Stanley Cohen named the pattern in Folk Devils and Moral Panics (1972), a study of the alarm over clashes between the youth groups known as Mods and Rockers at English seaside towns in the 1960s. A group or condition is defined as a threat; the press amplifies it with simple, vivid images and creates "folk devils"; public anxiety rises; editors, clergy, experts and politicians respond, often with new rules; then the panic fades. In 1994 Erich Goode and Nachman Ben-Yehuda listed five marks: concern, hostility toward the folk devil, broad agreement that the threat is real, disproportion between fear and harm, and volatility.

These cases fit parts of the model. The Serbian reports moved from village fear to military paperwork to a press debate across Europe. The Gévaudan beast became a national story. Werewolf courts found folk devils in outsiders such as the hermit Garnier. A later case, the satanic ritual abuse scare of the 1980s and early 1990s, produced thousands of allegations in North America and Britain; a 1994 study for the British government by the anthropologist Jean La Fontaine found no evidence of the satanic abuse rings alleged.

The fit is imperfect, and scholars warn against stretching it. "Panic" can suggest that the fear was baseless, but the deaths in Medveđa, Exeter and the Gévaudan were real; what was wrong was the explanation. Most people who opened graves acted within their communities' reasoning about contagion and the dead. Disproportion is also hard to measure: by what standard is a dying family's response excessive?
